CALIFORNIA ELECTRONIC COMMUNICATIONS PRIVACY ACT (CALECPA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Electronic Communications Privacy Act (CalECPA), California Penal Code §§ 1546-1546.4, enacted in 2015 (SB 178) and last amended in 2017 (SB 811, operative January 1, 2018). CalECPA generally requires a government entity to obtain a warrant, or to proceed under one of a small number of other enumerated legal-process options, before compelling a service provider to produce electronic communication information, or before accessing electronic device information — whether that information is held by a third-party service provider or physically on a device. This document states facts about the statutory text currently in effect, together with one published California appellate decision applying it, regarding Taylor Morgan and, where applicable, Acme, Inc. It does not evaluate whether any specific request, warrant, subpoena, or other demand for information concerning Taylor Morgan or Acme, Inc. complies with CalECPA or any other law, and does not address whether to consent to, comply with, or challenge any specific government request.

TWO STATUTORY CATEGORIES: “ELECTRONIC COMMUNICATION INFORMATION” AND “ELECTRONIC DEVICE INFORMATION”
CalECPA's core protections turn on two separately defined categories of information, both housed in the broader term “electronic information” (Penal Code § 1546(h)). “Electronic communication information” covers information about a communication or about the use of a communication service — content, sender, recipients, timing, and similar details, including an IP address. “Electronic device information” instead covers information stored on or generated by a device itself, including the device's current and prior locations. The statute applies different rules to compelling this information from a service provider versus accessing it by physically or electronically interacting with a device, as described in later clauses of this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "“Electronic communication information” means any information about an electronic communication or the use of an electronic communication service, including, but not limited to, the contents, sender, recipients, format, or location of the sender or recipients at any point during the communication, the time or date the communication was created, sent, or received, or any information pertaining to any individual or device participating in the communication, including, but not limited to, an IP address."
  — California Penal Code § 1546(d), Cal. Penal Code § 1546(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.)
  "“Electronic device information” means any information stored on or generated through the operation of an electronic device, including the current and prior locations of the device."
  — California Penal Code § 1546(g), Cal. Penal Code § 1546(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.)
  Known gap: Both quotes below come from single paragraphs of the official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text that each contain an internal line break inserted mid-sentence by the page's own HTML formatting (after “...participating in the communication,” in subdivision (d), and after “means any” in subdivision (g)). Both quotes are reproduced here with that line break normalized to a single space; the underlying HTML was independently fetched twice, using two distinct User-Agent strings on separate requests, and the text inside each paragraph, including the line-break placement, was byte-for-byte identical both times, confirming the break is a stable artifact of the source's own formatting rather than fetch noise. Separately, this clause quotes only 2 of the 12 lettered definitions in Penal Code § 1546; it does not restate the statute's definitions of “adverse result,” “authorized possessor,” “electronic communication,” “electronic communication service,” “electronic device,” “government entity,” “service provider,” “specific consent,” or “subscriber information,” several of which matter to how the exceptions described elsewhere in this document actually apply. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current statutory text — not a claim about which law governs any reader's specific situation.

THE DEFAULT RULE: THREE THINGS A GOVERNMENT ENTITY MAY NOT DO
Subject to the exceptions described in later clauses of this document, CalECPA states that a government entity shall not do any of three things: compel the production of or access to electronic communication information from a service provider; compel the production of or access to electronic device information from any person or entity other than the device's authorized possessor; or access electronic device information by physically or electronically interacting with the device itself. The same subdivision separately states that this prohibition does not stop the intended recipient of a communication from voluntarily disclosing information about that communication to a government entity on the recipient's own initiative.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Compel the production of or access to electronic communication information from a service provider."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.1(a)(1), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.1(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.1.)
  "Compel the production of or access to electronic device information from any person or entity other than the authorized possessor of the device."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.1(a)(2), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.1(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.1.)
  "Access electronic device information by means of physical interaction or electronic communication with the electronic device."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.1(a)(3), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.1(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.1.)
  Known gap: The three quotes below are subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(2), and the first sentence of (a)(3) of the same statutory section, Penal Code § 1546.1 — they are treated here as one source, not independent corroboration of each other. This clause does not quote or describe (a)(3)'s second sentence (the intended-recipient voluntary-disclosure carve-out, summarized only in this clause's body text above) or the related service-provider voluntary-disclosure provisions and 90-day destruction duty in § 1546.1(f)-(g), which this document does not otherwise address. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current statutory text — not a claim about which law governs any reader's specific situation, and not a claim that any specific request concerning any particular person or company falls inside or outside this prohibition.

COMPELLING INFORMATION FROM A SERVICE PROVIDER: THE ENUMERATED PATHWAYS
CalECPA lists a closed set of circumstances under which a government entity may compel a service provider to produce electronic communication information (or compel production of electronic device information from someone other than the device's authorized possessor): a warrant, a wiretap order, an order for electronic reader records under the separate Reader Privacy Act (Civil Code § 1798.90), a non-criminal-investigation subpoena, or a pen register/trap-and-trace order. The subpoena pathway is narrower than the others: it is only available when the information is not sought to investigate or prosecute a criminal offense, and does not itself expand any subpoena authority that state law provides elsewhere.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "A government entity may compel the production of or access to electronic communication information from a service provider, or compel the production of or access to electronic device information from any person or entity other than the authorized possessor of the device only under the following circumstances:"
  — California Penal Code § 1546.1(b), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.1(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.1.)
  "Pursuant to a warrant issued pursuant to Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 1523) and subject to subdivision (d)."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.1(b)(1), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.1(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.1.)
  "Pursuant to a subpoena issued pursuant to existing state law, provided that the information is not sought for the purpose of investigating or prosecuting a criminal offense, and compelling the production of or access to the information via the subpoena is not otherwise prohibited by state or federal law."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.1(b)(4), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.1(b)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.1.)
  Known gap: The two operative quotes below are the introductory clause of Penal Code § 1546.1(b) and one of its five enumerated paragraphs, (b)(1); they are subdivisions of the same statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent corroboration. This clause does not independently quote or verify the text of (b)(2) (the wiretap-order pathway), (b)(3) (the electronic-reader-records pathway, which depends on the separate Civil Code § 1798.90 Reader Privacy Act — a statute this document does not otherwise describe or source), or (b)(5) (the pen register/trap-and-trace pathway); each is only summarized in this clause's body text from the same source page used for the quoted text. It also does not quote the second sentence of (b)(4), or subdivision (d)'s separate particularity and sealing requirements that a warrant obtained under this pathway must independently satisfy (addressed in part in this document's later remedies clause). This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current statutory text — not a claim about which law governs any reader's specific situation.

ACCESSING A DEVICE DIRECTLY: CONSENT AND EMERGENCY EXCEPTIONS
Separately from the pathways for compelling records from a service provider, CalECPA lists twelve specific circumstances under which a government entity may access electronic device information by physically or electronically interacting with the device itself. Among them: the specific consent of the device's authorized possessor; the specific consent of the device's owner, but only once the device has been reported lost or stolen (a narrower, owner-specific version of the consent exception); and a good-faith belief that an emergency involving danger of death or serious physical injury requires access to the device information.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "With the specific consent of the authorized possessor of the device."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.1(c)(4), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.1(c)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.1.)
  "With the specific consent of the owner of the device, only when the device has been reported as lost or stolen."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.1(c)(5), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.1(c)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.1.)
  "If the government entity, in good faith, believes that an emergency involving danger of death or serious physical injury to any person requires access to the electronic device information."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.1(c)(6), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.1(c)(6) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.1.)

The (c)(6) quote is reproduced with an internal line break — inserted mid-sentence, after “believes that,” by the source page's own HTML formatting — normalized to a single space; the underlying page was independently fetched twice with two distinct User-Agent strings, and the paragraph's text, including that line-break placement, was byte-for-byte identical both times. This clause covers only 3 of subdivision (c)'s 12 enumerated exceptions; it does not quote or describe the warrant, wiretap-order, or tracking-device-warrant pathways in (c)(1)-(3), the lost-or-abandoned-device exception in (c)(7), the correctional-facility, parole, or probation/pretrial-release exceptions in (c)(8)-(10), or the 911-emergency-call location exception in (c)(11); each is a distinct, separately conditioned exception this document does not independently verify. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current statutory text — not a claim about which law governs any reader's specific situation, and not a claim that any specific access to a device belonging to or possessed by any particular reader falls inside or outside any exception.

NOTICE TO THE TARGET, AND THE COURT'S POWER TO DELAY IT
When a government entity executes a warrant, or obtains electronic information in an emergency, CalECPA requires it to serve the identified targets with a notice stating that their information was compelled or obtained and describing the investigation with reasonable specificity, along with a copy of the warrant or a written statement of the emergency facts. Notice must ordinarily be provided contemporaneously with executing a warrant, or within three court days of an emergency disclosure. A court may instead delay that notice on the government entity's sworn-affidavit request, but only upon finding reason to believe notice would cause an adverse result, and only for a period not to exceed 90 days at a time — though the statute lets a court grant repeated 90-day extensions on the same grounds, without stating any cap on how many extensions may be granted.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Except as otherwise provided in this section, any government entity that executes a warrant, or obtains electronic information in an emergency pursuant to Section 1546.1, shall serve upon, or deliver to by registered or first-class mail, electronic mail, or other means reasonably calculated to be effective, the identified targets of the warrant or emergency access, a notice that informs the recipient that information about the recipient has been compelled or obtained, and states with reasonable specificity the nature of the government investigation under which the information is sought."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.2(a)(1), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.2(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.2.)
  "The notice shall be provided contemporaneously with the execution of a warrant, or, in the case of an emergency, within three court days after obtaining the electronic information."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.2(a)(1) (timing), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.2(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.2.)
  "The court shall issue the order if the court determines that there is reason to believe that notification may have an adverse result, but only for the period of time that the court finds there is reason to believe that the notification may have that adverse result, and not to exceed 90 days."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.2(b)(1), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.2(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.2.)
  "The court may grant extensions of the delay of up to 90 days each on the same grounds as provided in paragraph (1)."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.2(b)(2), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.2(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.2.)
  Known gap: The four quotes below come from Penal Code § 1546.2, subdivisions (a)(1) and (b)(1)-(2); they are treated as one source, not independent corroboration of each other. Two of the four — the (a)(1) timing sentence and all of (b)(1) — are reproduced with an internal line break, inserted mid-sentence by the source page's own HTML formatting, normalized to a single space; the underlying page was independently fetched twice with two distinct User-Agent strings, and each paragraph's text, including the line-break placement, was byte-for-byte identical both times. This clause does not address subdivision (a)(2)'s exception to notice for a 911 emergency location request, subdivision (b)(3)'s requirement for what the notice must contain once a delay period expires, or subdivision (c)'s Department of Justice reporting duty when a warrant or emergency access has no identified target. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current statutory text — not a claim about which law governs any reader's specific situation, and not a claim that notice to notice to any particular person was or was not given, delayed, or required in any specific instance.

AVAILABLE REMEDIES, AND WHAT ONE PUBLISHED CASE SAYS THEY DO (AND DON'T) GUARANTEE
CalECPA gives a person in a trial, hearing, or proceeding the right to move to suppress electronic information obtained or retained in violation of the Fourth Amendment or of the statute itself, using the same procedures that already govern other search-warrant suppression motions. Separately, an individual whose information is targeted by a warrant, order, or other legal process inconsistent with the statute or the state or federal constitution — or a service provider or other recipient of such process — may petition the issuing court to void or modify it, or to order destruction of information obtained in violation of it. A 2023 published California Court of Appeal decision, People v. Meza, applied CalECPA's particularity requirement to a geofence warrant and illustrates two distinct limits on what these remedies guarantee in practice: the court found the warrant satisfied CalECPA's own statutory particularity requirement, but nonetheless violated the separate, stricter particularity requirement of the Fourth Amendment — and even so, declined to suppress the evidence because the federal good-faith exception applied.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Any person in a trial, hearing, or proceeding may move to suppress any electronic information obtained or retained in violation of the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution or of this chapter."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.4(a), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.4(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.4.)
  "An individual whose information is targeted by a warrant, order, or other legal process that is inconsistent with this chapter, or the California Constitution or the United States Constitution, or a service provider or any other recipient of the warrant, order, or other legal process may petition the issuing court to void or modify the warrant, order, or process, or to order the destruction of any information obtained in violation of this chapter, or the California Constitution, or the United States Constitution."
  — California Penal Code § 1546.4(c), Cal. Penal Code § 1546.4(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1546.4.)
  "Although the geofence warrant satisfied the requirements of CalECPA, we agree it lacked the particularity required by the Fourth Amendment and was impermissibly overbroad. Nonetheless, we affirm Meza’s and Meneses’s convictions under the good faith exception to the exclusionary rule established by United States v. Leon (1984) 468 U.S. 897 (Leon)."
  — People v. Meza, 90 Cal.App.5th 520 (Cal. Ct. App. 2023) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9421025/people-v-meza/)

The (c) quote is reproduced with an internal line break, inserted mid-sentence by the source page's own HTML formatting, normalized to a single space; the underlying page was independently fetched twice with two distinct User-Agent strings and the paragraph's text, including the line-break placement, was byte-for-byte identical both times. Meza: CourtListener's own citation metadata for this specific opinion record returned an empty citation list; the reporter citation used here, 90 Cal.App.5th 520, was instead confirmed from the opinion's own internal cross-references to itself (a later dissenting statement from denial of review, reproduced in the same record, cites “Meza, supra, 90 Cal.App.5th at p. 526”). The California Supreme Court denied review of this decision, over a published dissenting statement by Justice Liu; a denial of review is not the Supreme Court's approval of the Court of Appeal's reasoning, and this document does not track whether any other California appellate court has since followed, distinguished, or criticized Meza's particularity or good-faith-exception holdings, or how they apply outside the geofence-warrant context in which the case arose. This case and statute are evidence of California's current law on this point — not a claim about the outcome of any specific reader's situation.

This information sheet regarding California's Electronic Communications Privacy Act (Penal Code §§ 1546-1546.4) was provided by Acme, Inc. to Taylor Morgan on September 8, 2026, and was prepared by Jordan T. Receipt and review of this information sheet does not itself constitute a request, consent, warrant, or legal process of any kind, and this information sheet does not itself determine whether any specific request, warrant, subpoena, or other demand for information concerning Taylor Morgan or Acme, Inc. complies with this statute or any other law.

expectedJSON.body: CalECPA gives a person in a trial, hearing, or proceeding the right to move to suppress electronic information obtained or retained in violation of the Fourth Amendment or of the statute itself, using the same procedures that already govern other search-warrant suppression motions. Separately, an individual whose information is targeted by a warrant, order, or other legal process inconsistent with the statute or the state or federal constitution — or a service provider or other recipient of such process — may petition the issuing court to void or modify it, or to order destruction of information obtained in violation of it. A 2023 published California Court of Appeal decision, People v. Meza, applied CalECPA's particularity requirement to a geofence warrant and illustrates two distinct limits on what these remedies guarantee in practice: the court found the warrant satisfied CalECPA's own statutory particularity requirement, but nonetheless violated the separate, stricter particularity requirement of the Fourth Amendment — and even so, declined to suppress the evidence because the federal good-faith exception applied.

citations.quote: Any person in a trial, hearing, or proceeding may move to suppress any electronic information obtained or retained in violation of the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution or of this chapter.

An individual whose information is targeted by a warrant, order, or other legal process that is inconsistent with this chapter, or the California Constitution or the United States Constitution, or a service provider or any other recipient of the warrant, order, or other legal process may petition the issuing court to void or modify the warrant, order, or process, or to order the destruction of any information obtained in violation of this chapter, or the California Constitution, or the United States Constitution.

Although the geofence warrant satisfied the requirements of CalECPA, we agree it lacked the particularity required by the Fourth Amendment and was impermissibly overbroad. Nonetheless, we affirm Meza’s and Meneses’s convictions under the good faith exception to the exclusionary rule established by United States v. Leon (1984) 468 U.S. 897 (Leon).
